intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-42B (DEE42B) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the CACNA1A gene (601011) on chromosome 19p13.13.

checks.claim: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-42B (DEE42B) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the CACNA1A gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Compound heterozygous mutations in the CACNA1A gene presumably cause early onset epileptic encephalopathy, and progressive cerebral, cerebellar and optic nerve atrophy with reduced lifespan.
checks.explanation: The paper reports only compound heterozygous mutations. It does not mention homozygous mutations.

checks.claim: The CACNA1A gene is located on chromosome 19p13.13.
checks.evidence_quote: The CACNA1A gene encodes the transmembrane pore-forming alpha-1A subunit of the Cav 2.1 P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channel.
checks.explanation: The abstract does not give the chromosomal location. This is standard gene nomenclature, which the rules count as restating the paper.

paragraphs.text: DEE42B is a severe autosomal recessive neurologic disorder. Seizures begin in early infancy and are accompanied by profound hypotonia, global developmental delay, and visual impairment with optic atrophy. Brain imaging shows progressive cerebral and cerebellar atrophy, and lifespan is reduced. Reinson et al. (2016) concluded that compound heterozygous CACNA1A mutations presumably cause early-onset epileptic encephalopathy with progressive cerebral, cerebellar, and optic nerve atrophy and reduced lifespan.

checks.claim: DEE42B is a severe autosomal recessive neurologic disorder.
checks.evidence_quote: Biallelic CACNA1A mutations cause early onset epileptic encephalopathy with progressive cerebral, cerebellar, and optic nerve atrophy.
checks.explanation: The paper describes a severe biallelic disorder but never uses the term 'autosomal recessive'.

paragraphs.text: Reinson et al. (2016) reported a sister and brother. Both were normal at birth but developed daily recurrent seizures in early infancy, together with extreme muscular hypotonia, hypokinesia, and global developmental delay. Brain MRI showed progressive cerebral, cerebellar, and optic nerve atrophy. At age 5 years, both patients were blind and bedridden with profound developmental delay. The elder sister died at that age.

paragraphs.text: Wong-Spracklen et al. (2022) reported a White British girl born to nonconsanguineous parents and followed to age 10 years. She had infantile hypotonia with a weak suck. Seizures began at 6 months, and she later had tonic-clonic status epilepticus, drug-resistant generalized tonic-clonic seizures, tonic seizures, and myoclonus. Poor bulbar function required gastrostomy, and she had recurrent chest infections, respiratory arrests, and drooling. Other findings were: - secondary microcephaly - fixed flexion contractures of the elbows, hips, and knees - no purposeful movement and inability to sit unsupported at 3 years - an alternating convergent squint and delayed visual maturation - impaired social function - severe intellectual disability, with a Vineland Adaptive Scales composite score of 26 She had no spasticity and no dysmorphic features. MRI at 6 months showed mild cerebellar hypoplasia and a thin corpus callosum. MRI at 3 years showed cerebellar volume loss involving both hemispheres, the vermis, and the middle cerebellar peduncles, and mildly prominent ventricles and extraaxial CSF spaces reflecting mild cerebral volume loss. EEG showed continuous focal sharp and slow wave complexes over the posterior regions. Nerve conduction, EMG, ERG, audiology, and a metabolic screen were normal.

paragraphs.text: Mammadova et al. (2024) reported a family in which 3 of 4 boys born to nonconsanguineous parents were severely affected. The index patient (II-4) had neonatal muscular hypotonia, and his first seizures occurred at 4 weeks of age. He developed early-onset epileptic encephalopathy with severe muscular hypotonia, absent deep tendon reflexes, and respiratory and swallowing insufficiency requiring tube feeding. His seizures were highly frequent and refractory, and included bilateral clonic seizures, myoclonic seizures, and ictal apneic spells. EEG showed burst suppression, and later generalized background slowing with multifocal sharp waves. He had severe global developmental delay, blindness, and optic atrophy, but cerebral MRI was normal. He died at 2.5 years. His brother (II-2) had muscular hypotonia from the first week of life, and seizures began at 5 months. He had hypsarrhythmia, deep apneic spells, and refractory seizures, together with severe developmental impairment, blindness, optic atrophy, edema, and dysphagia requiring tube feeding. Respiratory problems required mechanical ventilation. Imaging showed cerebellar hypoplasia. PEHO (progressive encephalopathy, edema, hypsarrhythmia, optic atrophy) syndrome had been suspected on clinical grounds. He died at 14 months. The eldest brother (II-1) had neonatal-onset muscular hypotonia and severe developmental impairment. He died at 5 months with suspected sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS). Mammadova et al. (2024) proposed that ictal apneic spells were the most prominent seizure type and the probable cause of death in the affected sibs. They suggested that the sib diagnosed with SIDS probably died of ictal apnea.

paragraphs.text: The transmission pattern of DEE42B in the families reported by Reinson et al. (2016), Wong-Spracklen et al. (2022), and Mammadova et al. (2024) was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance. Arteche-López et al. (2021) suggested that codominant or recessive inheritance could explain why patients with a homozygous loss-of-function CACNA1A variant differed from patients with the dominant CACNA1A phenotypes.

checks.claim: The transmission pattern of DEE42B in the family reported by Reinson et al. (2016) was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.
checks.evidence_quote: Their parents and two siblings were heterozygotes for one of those pathogenic mutations
checks.explanation: Affected sibs with biallelic mutations and carrier parents fit recessive transmission, which follows directly from what the paper states.

checks.claim: The transmission pattern of DEE42B in the family reported by Wong-Spracklen et al. (2022) was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.
checks.evidence_quote: This case illustrates the potential for a recessive diagnosis in an apparently sporadic disorder in which a de novo cause is initially considered more likely.
checks.explanation: Compound heterozygous variants were inherited one from each parent.

checks.claim: The transmission pattern of DEE42B in the family reported by Mammadova et al. (2024) was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.
checks.evidence_quote: CACNA1 therefore belongs to the growing list of genes with co-dominantly or both autosomal dominantly and autosomal recessively inherited diseases.
checks.explanation: Affected sibs are compound heterozygous for variants inherited from heterozygous parents, which fits recessive inheritance.

checks.claim: Arteche-López et al. (2021) suggested that codominant or recessive inheritance could explain why patients with a homozygous loss-of-function CACNA1A variant differed from patients with dominant CACNA1A phenotypes.
checks.evidence_quote: We suggest that co-dominant or recessive inheritance for these three genes could explain the phenotypic differences from those documented in their cognate dominant phenotypes.
checks.explanation: The abstract makes this suggestion about all three genes, CACNA1A included.

paragraphs.text: Heterozygous carriers in these families had variable phenotypes. Reinson et al. (2016) found that the heterozygous parents and 2 heterozygous sibs had a milder phenotype that included intellectual disability. In contrast, Wong-Spracklen et al. (2022) noted that the heterozygous carrier parents of their patient did not show clear signs of a CACNA1A-associated syndrome. They noted that this complicated segregation analysis and genetic counseling and left uncertainty about whether the recurrence risk was 25% or 50%. In the family reported by Mammadova et al. (2024), the heterozygous carriers were either asymptomatic or had milder neurologic phenotypes. The authors concluded that CACNA1A belongs to the genes associated with both autosomal dominant and autosomal recessive disease.

checks.claim: Heterozygous CACNA1A carriers in DEE42B families had variable phenotypes.
checks.evidence_quote: However, family members with heterozygous CACNA1A variants are either asymptomatic or have mild and non‐specific features. Reduced penetrance and high degrees of intra‐familial variability have been reported across all CACNA1A phenotypes.
checks.explanation: The paper also contrasts this family with others in which carriers had ID/ataxia or EA2.

checks.claim: Reinson et al. (2016) found that the heterozygous parents and 2 heterozygous sibs of the DEE42B patients had a milder phenotype that included intellectual disability.

paragraphs.text: In 2 affected brothers (II-4 and II-2) with DEE42B, Mammadova et al. (2024) identified compound heterozygous frameshift variants in the CACNA1A gene (NM_001127222.1): c.2602delG (Ala868ProfsTer24) and c.5476delC (His1826ThrfsTer30). The variants were found by exome sequencing in the index patient (II-4) and confirmed in material from his deceased brother (II-2). The c.2602delG variant was inherited from the mother and c.5476delC from the father. The mother and a maternal uncle, who both carried c.2602delG, had episodic ataxia type 2. The father, who carried c.5476delC, was asymptomatic. Material from the eldest affected brother (II-1) was not available for testing. A fourth brother (II-3) was reported in the text to be heterozygous for the maternal c.2602delG variant, although Table 1 of the report lists him as heterozygous for the paternal c.5476delC variant. He had a milder phenotype: primary generalized epilepsy beginning at 5 years with atypical absences, mild intellectual impairment, episodic unsteady gait, dizziness, attention deficit-hyperactivity disorder, and mild muscular hypotonia, with normal cranial MRI.

paragraphs.text: Mammadova et al. (2024) suggested that biallelic truncating CACNA1A variants are associated with severe early-onset epileptic encephalopathy with a fatal outcome. They contrasted this with longer survival in patients who are compound heterozygous for a missense and a truncating variant, and with late-onset myoclonic epilepsy in a patient with a homozygous in-frame variant. paragraphs.text: In 2 brothers with DEE42B, Mammadova et al. (2024) identified compound heterozygous frameshift variants in the CACNA1A gene (NM_001127222.1). One was a 1-bp deletion (c.5476delC) predicted to result in a frameshift (His1826ThrfsTer30), and the other was c.2602delG. The variants were found by exome sequencing. The c.5476delC variant was inherited from the father, who was asymptomatic.

checks.claim: Mammadova et al. (2024) identified compound heterozygous frameshift CACNA1A variants (NM_001127222.1) in 2 brothers with DEE42B.
checks.evidence_quote: Exome sequencing revealed compound heterozygosity for two pathogenic CACNA1A (NM_001127222.1) variants in the index patient (II-4). Exome sequencing also confirmed these two variants in material from deceased child II-2.
